days.t: In Spain the Three Wise Men, not Santa, bring most of the presents. The evening before, towns hold parades (cabalgatas) throwing sweets, and families share a roscón de Reyes cake with a hidden figurine.
Huge, satirical sculptures of wood and papier-mâché fill Valencia's streets, and on the night of 19 March almost all of them are burnt in the cremà.
Holy Week brings processions with heavy floats (pasos) carried through the streets; Seville and Málaga are famous for them.
On St George's day, Catalans give each other books and roses; the streets of Barcelona fill with book and flower stalls. It's also the day Cervantes is remembered.
On the shortest night of the year, people light bonfires on beaches and in squares and jump over them; in some places you make a wish and jump over seven waves.
The festival runs from 6 to 14 July: people in white with red scarves, music day and night, and the famous early-morning encierros, the running of the bulls.
On the last Wednesday of August, thousands of people throw tomatoes at each other for one hour in this small town near Valencia.
Spain's national day, with a military parade in Madrid; it also marks 12 October 1492, when Columbus reached the Americas.
Families visit cemeteries to bring flowers to their loved ones, and eat sweets like buñuelos and huesos de santo.
The children of the San Ildefonso school sing the winning numbers on live TV for hours; many people share tickets with friends, family and colleagues.
Spain's version of April Fools' Day: people play pranks, and newspapers publish fake stories.
At midnight people eat twelve grapes, one with each chime of the clock at Puerta del Sol in Madrid, for good luck in each month of the new year.

facts: Spanish is the official language of 20 countries and the second most spoken native language in the world.
In Spain lunch is usually eaten between 2 and 3 pm and dinner often after 9 pm.
The Sagrada Família in Barcelona, designed by Gaudí, has been under construction since 1882.
Spain has four co-official languages besides Spanish in their regions: Catalan, Galician, Basque and Aranese (Occitan).
Basque (euskera) is not related to any other known language in the world.
Don Quixote, by Miguel de Cervantes, published in 1605, is often called the first modern novel.
The Golden Age (Siglo de Oro), around the 16th and 17th centuries, gave Spain painters like Velázquez and writers like Lope de Vega and Quevedo.
The siesta is less common than people think: most Spaniards work through the afternoon, but shops in small towns may still close for a few hours.
The Alhambra in Granada was the palace of the last Muslim kingdom in the peninsula, which ended in 1492.
Tapas may have started as a slice of bread or ham used to 'cover' (tapar) a glass of wine.
Spain has more than 45 UNESCO World Heritage sites, one of the highest numbers in the world.
Flamenco, from Andalusia, combines song (cante), guitar (toque) and dance (baile); it is UNESCO Intangible Heritage.
The Camino de Santiago is a network of pilgrimage routes to Santiago de Compostela walked since the Middle Ages.
Many words in Spanish come from Arabic, like aceite (oil), azúcar (sugar) and ojalá (hopefully).
In Spain, people usually have two surnames: the first from their father and the second from their mother (the order can now be chosen).
The Prado Museum in Madrid holds masterpieces like Las Meninas by Velázquez and The Garden of Earthly Delights by Bosch.
In Spain, greeting friends with two kisses on the cheeks (dos besos) is normal, starting with the right cheek.
At about 650 metres above sea level, Madrid is one of the highest capitals in Europe.
Paella comes from Valencia; the original recipe has chicken, rabbit and beans, not seafood.
Spain's Christmas season lasts until 6 January, Three Kings' Day.

places.d: The capital, in the centre of the peninsula, with the Prado Museum, the Royal Palace and the Retiro park.
places.food: Cocido madrileño, bocadillo de calamares and churros with chocolate.
places.cos: On Sundays, El Rastro flea market fills the streets of La Latina.
places.eti: Polite: greeting with dos besos among friends. Rude: rushing people at lunch; meals are long.
places.dia: Madrid Spanish is close to the standard; people from Madrid are called madrileños, or gatos (cats).

places.d: Mediterranean city of Gaudí: the Sagrada Família, Park Güell and Casa Batlló.
places.food: Pa amb tomàquet (bread with tomato), crema catalana and calçots in spring.
places.cos: Human towers (castells) are built at festivals; they are UNESCO heritage.
places.eti: Catalan is co-official: a simple 'bon dia' or 'gràcies' is appreciated.
places.dia: Catalan is a separate Romance language, spoken alongside Spanish.

places.d: Andalusian capital with the Giralda, the Alcázar and the Plaza de España.
places.food: Gazpacho, salmorejo, fried fish and tapas.
places.cos: The April Fair (Feria de Abril) is a week of flamenco dresses, sevillanas and casetas.
places.eti: Andalusians are open and chatty; joining a conversation at the bar is normal.
places.dia: Andalusian Spanish drops final s ('¿cómo estás?' sounds like 'cómo ehtá') and often says 'ustedes' instead of 'vosotros'.

places.d: Home of the Alhambra, palace of the last Muslim kingdom of al-Andalus (until 1492).
places.food: Free tapas with every drink, and piononos from nearby Santa Fe.
places.cos: From the Mirador de San Nicolás people watch the sunset over the Alhambra.
places.eti: Ordering one drink each round is normal: each one comes with a new free tapa.

places.d: Mediterranean city of the City of Arts and Sciences and the Fallas festival.
places.food: Paella valenciana (chicken, rabbit, green beans) and horchata with fartons.
places.cos: Real paella is cooked on a wood fire and eaten at lunchtime, not dinner.
places.eti: Never call any rice with things in it 'paella' in front of a Valencian.
places.dia: Valencian (a form of Catalan) is co-official.

places.d: End of the Camino de Santiago pilgrimage, in rainy, green Galicia.
places.food: Pulpo á feira (octopus with paprika), empanada gallega and tarta de Santiago.
places.cos: Pilgrims arriving at the cathedral receive the Compostela certificate.
places.eti: Galicians are said to answer a question with another question.
places.dia: Galician (galego), close to Portuguese, is co-official.

places.d: The Basque Country: the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao and the bay of La Concha.
places.food: Pintxos (small bites on bread), bacalao al pil-pil and Basque cheesecake.
places.cos: Txokos are gastronomic societies where members cook together.
places.eti: With pintxos, you take what you want and tell the waiter at the end: honesty is expected.
places.dia: Basque (euskera) is unrelated to any other known language: 'kaixo' means hello.

places.d: Its university, founded in 1218, is the oldest in Spain still running; the Plaza Mayor is one of the most beautiful.
places.food: Hornazo (meat pie) and Iberian ham from nearby Guijuelo.
places.cos: Students look for the little frog carved on the university façade for good luck.
places.eti: Using 'usted' with older people is a sign of respect.
places.dia: Castilian Spanish of Salamanca is often considered very 'clear'.

places.d: The 'city of three cultures', where Christians, Muslims and Jews lived side by side in the Middle Ages.
places.cos: Toledo has been famous for its swords and damascene metalwork for centuries.
places.eti: Visiting churches: dress modestly and speak quietly.

places.d: Volcanic islands off Africa with Mount Teide, Spain's highest peak (3,715 m).
places.food: Papas arrugadas with mojo sauce and gofio.
places.cos: On La Gomera, people still use silbo, a whistled language, to talk across valleys.
places.eti: Canarians use 'ustedes' instead of 'vosotros', like in Latin America.
places.dia: Canarian Spanish sounds close to Caribbean Spanish: 'guagua' means bus.

figures.t: Queen who, with Ferdinand of Aragon, united the crowns of Spain and sponsored Columbus' voyage in 1492.
Mystic, writer and reformer of the Carmelite order; one of the great writers of Spanish prose.
Author of Don Quixote; he fought at the battle of Lepanto and was a captive in Algiers for five years.
Court painter of Philip IV; his Las Meninas is one of the most studied paintings in history.
Painter of the royal court and of the horrors of war; his 'Black Paintings' anticipated modern art.
Catalan architect of the Sagrada Família, Park Güell and Casa Batlló.
Poet and playwright from Granada (Gypsy Ballads, Blood Wedding), killed at the start of the Civil War.
Lawyer and member of parliament who won women's right to vote in Spain in 1931.

words.t: A summer street party in a Spanish neighbourhood or village, with music, dancing and food late into the night.
The town square, the heart of every Spanish town: people meet there to chat, eat and celebrate.
A shepherds’ dish of fried breadcrumbs with garlic and chorizo, sometimes served with grapes.
In Andalusia, the inner courtyard full of flower pots. Córdoba holds a patio festival every May.
The time spent chatting at the table after a meal. There is no single English word for it.
Small dishes shared with a drink. In some cities they come free with what you order.
The afternoon snack around 5–6 pm, often a sandwich (bocadillo) or bread with chocolate.
The Three Wise Men bring Spanish children their presents on the night of 5 January.
Fried dough sticks dipped in thick hot chocolate, a classic breakfast or snack.
A short nap after lunch, during the hottest hours of the day.
